courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
md: Never write secrets into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists data to exclude or mask: passwords, access tokens, session identifiers (hash them if you need to follow a session), encryption keys, connection strings and sensitive personal data. Logs are copied widely, so anything in them leaks widely.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
md: Every allowlist entry is a promise that this pattern will never be malicious. Prefer fields the attacker cannot set (exact path in a protected folder, code-signing publisher, asset group from your inventory) over fields they can (process name, command-line text, user agent, file name).

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Do not trust a single number. Low perplexity, a passing passkey test and a large advertised window can all coexist with poor use of mid-context information. Test retrieval at many depths, multi-hop and aggregation tasks, and short-context regressions.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop
md: Random iteration counts teach one set of weights to work at many depths. Truncated backprop through only the last $k$ iterations keeps training memory independent of $r$, while the input injection still sends gradient to the prelude.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA does not compress or approximate the pretrained weight. W0 keeps all its information at full rank. Only the *change* learned during fine-tuning is restricted to rank r.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Composing adapters: switching, merging and task arithmetic
md: Adapters compose. Switch with set_adapter, recover the base for free with disable_adapter (a free reference model for DPO), and merge with task arithmetic, TIES or DARE. Combine whole updates $s\,BA$, never the A's and B's separately: cat is exact, linear is not.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Quarantine and Gatekeeper: the first-launch check
md: Gatekeeper is a first-launch, quarantine-triggered check. Removing the attribute (`xattr -d`), fetching with `curl`, or running a script through `bash` or `osascript` means it is never asked. Treat a process tree of browser or chat app, then Terminal, then curl, then shell or osascript as a detection signal, not as something Gatekeeper already covered.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: FileVault, secure boot and startup security
md: The SSV, SIP and FileVault protect each other. Apple notes the system will not let a user turn off the signed system volume while FileVault is on, because a tampered OS could capture the password at next boot. A baseline should require Full Security, SIP, SSV and FileVault together, and MDM should report any Mac that drops one.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Triage: hashes, magic bytes and strings
md: Strings lie by omission. Serious malware encrypts or encodes its strings and builds them at run time, so a short, clean strings list is not evidence of innocence. A file with almost no readable text at all is itself suspicious, as the packing lesson shows.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Packing, obfuscation and entropy
md: High entropy is a signal, not a verdict. Installers, compressed images in resources, and legitimately UPX-packed tools are high entropy too. Combine it with other signs: few imports, a writable and executable section, a raw size much smaller than the virtual size, or a section name that is not one of the usual ones.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
md: When you combine a prefix with int8, compute the calibration ranges on the vectors you actually store and query: the re-normalized prefixes. Re-normalizing a 64-d prefix of a 768-d unit vector makes its entries about 2.5 times larger for nomic-embed-text-v1.5, so ranges taken from the full vectors clip many of them. Lesson 8 measures the effect.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
md: Every knob in this course trades three things: memory per GPU, communication on a specific link, and idle or redundant compute. MFU is the single number that tells you whether the trade worked.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: VADs and malfind: finding code that has no file
md: A clean malfind proves little too. Code injected into an EXECUTE_READ region with a properly mapped file, or code that hides its pages while sleeping (lesson 12), will not match these rules. Use malfind with the other views, never alone.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Internal fragmentation is waste inside handed-out blocks (a rounding cost). External fragmentation is free memory split into holes too small to use (a placement and lifetime cost). Both are measured against live data, and the number depends on when you measure.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: There is no "acquire store" or "release load". Release only affects stores and Acquire only affects loads; SeqCst cannot create them either. A Release store and a Release store never synchronize with each other.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: EBR pays per operation, not per node, and needs no per-node announcement. In exchange, a single thread stalled while pinned blocks all reclamation, so garbage is unbounded.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: The call stack: frames, return addresses and saved frame pointers
md: The stack grows toward lower addresses, so people often assume an overflowing array also spills downward. It does not. `strcpy`, `gets` and loops write from `buf[0]` toward `buf[7]` and beyond, which means toward *higher* addresses: straight into the saved frame pointer and the return address of the same frame.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: Re-ID is open-set retrieval: open-set means the people at test time are not among the training classes. You do not predict a label; you learn distances that rank true matches first for people the model has never seen.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: Misconception: "warm-up makes a benchmark more accurate". It makes it measure **steady state**. If your function really runs once per request on cold caches, the warmed number is precise and wrong. Decide which regime production is in, then measure that one.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Launching and watching a Miles run
md: Architecture flags are not self-validating. Two checkpoints of one family can ship a different `--rotary-base`, vocab padding or norm epsilon. Diff the checkpoint's `config.json` against its file in `scripts/models/` before a first run and append any drifted value, for example `--extra-args "--rotary-base 10000"`.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
md: Misconception: "we never exported that activity, so it is not exported." Libraries add components to the merged manifest at build time. Review the manifest of the APK you ship (lesson 3), not the one in your repository.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: Cache size per token is set by what you store per token per layer. MQA and GQA shrink it by sharing keys and values across heads. MLA's bet is different: store one small learned vector per token and let each head derive its own keys and values from it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Many GPUs, many tenants: placement, cold starts and fairness
md: At cluster scale, multi-LoRA serving is a placement problem: consolidate load (Punica), switch merged and unmerged as traffic skews (dLoRA), hide adapter loads (prefetch, async or CPU-assisted prefill), and schedule for fairness across tenants, not only for throughput.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Why states hack: five purposes behind state operations
md: Ask what the operation is *for* before asking who did it. Espionage, disruption, influence, pre-positioning and revenue each predict different targets, dwell times and signs of success, and so different defences.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Wartime cyber in Ukraine, 2022: wipers, a satellite network, the grid
md: A coincidence in time is not proof of coordination. Mandiant noted the overlap with missile strikes and explicitly declined to claim a link. When you build a timeline, keep "happened at the same time" and "was planned together" as separate statements, with separate evidence.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Choose by the edits you must survive. Resizes, recompression and tone changes: a perceptual hash with Hamming search is cheap and exact. Crops, overlays, rotations and composites: a learned copy descriptor with nearest neighbor search. Either way, tune the threshold on labeled pairs from your own traffic.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
md: Static ARP entries on every laptop are not a practical fix: they break when hardware changes and do not scale. Put the check in the switch (DHCP snooping plus DAI), where one configuration covers every port, and encrypt traffic so a successful poisoner learns little.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
md: A firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Firewalls decide who may talk to whom on which port; whether the conversation itself is malicious is the job of the application, TLS, and IDS or application-layer inspection.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
md: Every Suricata alert should send you to the flow behind it: pull the EVE records with the same flow_id (or the Zeek logs with the same Community ID) and decide from the full conversation, not from the alert message alone.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Network forensics is pivoting with discipline: logs to scope, packets to prove, one UTC timeline, every step recorded. The attacker controls the infected host; they rarely control your sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
md: "Block all ICMP" is a common overreaction. It hides hosts from ping sweeps, but it also breaks useful signals such as fragmentation needed (type 3, code 4), which hosts rely on to size their packets. Filter selectively: allow the error messages your network needs, rate-limit echo, and log the rest.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Setting a policy does not move pages that already exist. `mbind(2)` affects only new allocations unless you pass the flag `MPOL_MF_MOVE` (or `MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL`, which also moves pages that other processes share, and so needs CAP_SYS_NICE, a Linux capability: one of the slices of root privilege a process can hold). Install the policy before the first touch, or ask for migration explicitly.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
md: NVMe queue depth does not make flash faster; it lets the controller keep many dies busy. One synchronous 4 KB read at a time pays the full read latency per request no matter how many queues the drive has. Use async I/O (io_uring, the Linux asynchronous I/O interface built on shared submission and completion rings; SPDK, or many threads) to keep enough requests in flight.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: A density map gives a number, not a list of objects. You cannot crop, identify or follow an individual from it, and the count is real-valued. Use it when objects are too dense to box, not as a default.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: A common misconception: "we log everything, so we are observable". Logs scale with traffic times fields per event, metrics scale with the number of distinct label combinations, and traces scale with the sampling rate. Choosing where each fact lives is the design work.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: A common bug: cropping a single field, such as a price, and running Tesseract with the default `--psm 3`. Automatic page segmentation expects a page and can find no lines at all in a tight crop. Use `--psm 7` (one line) or `--psm 8` (one word), and leave a small white border around the text.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS cannot tell a harmless typo from a costly one: `42.50` predicted as `42.5` scores 0.8, the same as many genuine digit errors of similar size. For money and IDs, add field-level exact match after normalization.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
md: chroot changes how paths are looked up, nothing more. Open file descriptors, the working directory and root's privileges all ignore it. Real filesystem isolation needs a mount namespace, no privilege to undo it, and no handles that point outside.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Requirements and collection plans: decide before you search
md: No requirement, no collection. A plan that names sources, legal basis and retention keeps an investigation focused, defensible and small.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: Geolocate places and events, not private people. Working out where a private individual lives or goes from their photos is stalking, whatever the technique is called. Practise on public landmarks, games built for it, or published case studies.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: Never practise on real private people, including friends who "don't mind". Use public landmarks, fictional scenarios, practice platforms, and your own organisation with written permission.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history
md: Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: "Same problem" means the *same* failure, not just any failure. If removing a line turns a `StatisticsError` into a `NameError`, you did not shrink the bug; you created a new one. Compare the exception type and message every time, not just whether something crashed.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Prefill on top of a cached prefix, and sharing the compute too
md: A prefix hit turns prefill into a smaller prefill with an offset: new queries see a rectangle of cached keys plus a causal triangle, at positions that continue from the cache. Hits end on block boundaries and never include the last prompt token.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: what your DNS tells the world
md: Recon results drive scope questions, not actions. Finding that `vpn.example.com` exists does not make it in scope. Check the address against the scope guard before any active step.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
md: In `perf report`, a high Children value does not mean the function is doing the work. main is 100% in every program. Sort by Self to find what executes, by Children to find which caller to change.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Visibility and durability are different events. A store becomes visible when it reaches the coherent cache, and durable only when its line reaches the persistence domain. On ADR platforms, software must close that gap explicitly.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: SPF: which servers may send for a domain
md: Misconception: "SPF pass means the sender is who they claim". SPF pass means only that the connecting IP is allowed to send for the **envelope** domain. That domain may be the attacker's own.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Which end of a storage unit bit-fields start from, whether they may straddle units, and the signedness of a plain `int` bit-field are all implementation-defined in C (cppreference lists them). Two compilers or two ABIs can lay out the same bit-field struct differently, so never use bit-fields to match a wire format or a hardware register; use shifts and masks on a fixed-width integer instead.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A pose model's output is a fixed, ordered list of keypoints per person, each with a position and a confidence. Everything downstream (metrics, angles, rep counting) is arithmetic on that list.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Lattices from zero: points, bases and hard problems
md: The lattice trapdoor in one sentence: the **public key** is a pile of noisy equations, the **private key** is the secret that turns the noise back into something small, and encryption hides a message under more noise that only the key holder can strip away (next lesson, by hand).

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
md: Pre-filtering with a flat scan is exact and its cost is proportional to the number of matches, $sn$. That makes it the best plan for restrictive filters and the worst plan for broad ones.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: **The one thing to remember:** ask whether the next address is known before the current load finishes. If not, you are latency-bound and more bandwidth will not help. If yes, you are probably bandwidth-bound and the question becomes how many bytes you move.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: A hash of an identifier is an identifier. Anyone who can guess the input space (all phone numbers, all emails in a leaked list) can reverse it. Use a keyed HMAC for pseudonyms, and remember that pseudonymised data is still personal data.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: DP does not promise that nothing can be learned about you. If a study shows smoking causes cancer, a smoker's insurer learns something. DP promises that the result would have been about the same whether or not *your* data was in it.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: "We might need it later" is not a purpose. Data collected without a specified purpose fails GDPR Article 5(1)(b) and becomes an unreviewed liability in every copy.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Deleting the primary row is not erasure. Without a data map, copies in analytics, tickets, partners and backups survive, and the reply you sent the user is false.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket: why a hash works like a password
md: A hash or ticket is a password-equivalent. Protect where it is cached, make each one valid in as few places as possible, and watch for valid logons in the wrong context: right account, wrong machine, wrong protocol, wrong time.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: What should a step reward measure? Value, progress, implicit PRMs
md: Value says how promising a prefix is; progress (an advantage) says whether this step helped. Progress is the better step reward, if measured under a complementary prover. Implicit PRMs get Q values for free from an outcome model trained as a log ratio, and PRIME keeps that model fresh with online updates.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
md: Register save and restore is the same for every switch. The difference between a thread switch and a process switch is the address space: if `next` shares `prev`'s memory, the page table stays loaded and the TLB stays valid.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC
md: ADC = exact query, quantized database. Per query you build an $m \times k^*$ table once, then each database vector costs $m$ lookups and adds. This is why PQ scans are fast and why everyone uses ADC.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Sequence recovery is a proxy, not a goal. A design that recovers 100 percent of a natural sequence has designed nothing new, and a design that recovers 30 percent may fold perfectly well. Recovery is useful only because it correlates with getting the physics right. What you actually test is whether the designed sequence folds back to the backbone you asked for.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input
md: Read files with `with open(..., encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")`, put reusable steps in functions, and catch only the exceptions you can handle. A missing log is a finding, not a zero.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code
md: Data is never code. Parse it with a format-specific parser, pass it to other programs as list arguments, validate it against what it should be, and keep secrets in the environment, not in the file.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, "when the leader fails during a network partition") can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
md: A lock inside one process (threading.Lock here) protects only threads in that process. A web app with several worker processes or servers needs the lock where the state lives, usually in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Why "too fast to exploit" fails: jitter and the single-packet attack
md: The single-packet attack made network distance irrelevant: a tester far away can now hit a 1 ms window about as reliably as one on the same network. Treat every check-then-act as reachable, and fix it with atomicity, not with speed.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
md: A ranking model only knows what its feature vector tells it. If a signal that decides relevance (freshness for news, location for local search) is not encoded as a number for each query-document pair, no amount of model tuning can recover it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: ERR: a user who stops once satisfied
md: **$g_{\max}$ is a convention, and tools hard-code it.** TREC's `gdeval.pl` (the official Web track script, which ir_measures used for `ERR@5` in our test) sets `MAX_JUDGMENT = 4`. With our 0 to 3 grades, gdeval gives Run A an ERR@5 of 0.240, not 0.452, and Run B 0.438, not 0.875. Rankings of runs may survive, but the numbers cannot be compared with an ERR computed under $g_{\max} = 3$.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Change Healthcare and ALPHV, February 2024
md: One remote access portal without MFA, at one subsidiary, gave a criminal nine quiet days. Inventory every remote access path (VPNs, Citrix, RDP gateways, vendor portals, acquired companies' systems) and enforce MFA on all of them, then test that it is enforced.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Each server state is a statement about the past: "here is the world after your input #n". Reset to it, then replay inputs after #n. Sequence numbers are what make that subtraction possible.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
md: Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows
md: Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: A commit is only as safe as the set of machines that had it when the client was told "ok". Every replication knob is a choice of *how many* and *which* machines that set must include, paid for in commit latency.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: What RLHF reward hacking looks like: length, sycophancy, persuasion
md: Misconception: longer answers after RLHF just mean a more helpful model. Sometimes length carries real information. But when the reward gain mostly vanishes once you compare answers of equal length, the policy has optimized a correlate of quality, not quality. Report output length next to every reward and win rate.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: A common misconception: "security owns security risk". In every framework in this course, the **business owner** of a system owns its risk and the decision to accept it. The security team advises, measures and challenges. When security silently accepts risk on the business's behalf, nobody with budget or authority knows the risk exists.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
md: Every risk ends in one of four decisions, recorded with an owner and a date. Compare options in money: expected yearly loss plus treatment cost for the average, and tail percentiles for survival. Mitigation usually wins on average; insurance wins on the tail; avoidance can win on both.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: PCI DSS v4: the cardholder data environment and scoping
md: PCI DSS is a contractual standard with 12 requirements. Scope is the CDE plus anything connected to it or able to affect it, so reduce scope first: segment, and better, never touch card numbers (tokenise with a payment provider). What remains on your side, especially the payment page's scripts, must be inventoried and watched.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
md: Policies: short, owned, true, enforced by guardrails, with an exception path and a review date. Awareness: required by every framework, but measure it honestly; put the weight on controls that make human mistakes survivable, and on making reporting easy.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
md: Partial rollouts are not free. A trajectory stitched from segments generated by several policy versions is off-policy data. Kimi notes some segments can be excluded from the loss; AReaL's interruptible rollouts face the same issue and handle it with a modified PPO objective.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
md: Agentic rollouts move the bottleneck from decode length to tool latency. Run each trajectory as its own coroutine against continuous-batching servers, route a conversation's turns to the same server, scale tools as separate services, and pass exact token ids and logprobs to the trainer.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
md: Mitigating destroys evidence. Reverting the config drains the queue, restarts pods and rotates the logs that held the smoking gun. Before you revert, spend the 30 seconds: snapshot the pool metrics, grab one stack dump, copy the rendered config, note the exact timestamps. The chapter's phrase is that rapid triage does not preclude preserving evidence of what is going wrong.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Weighted RRF and multi-query fusion (RAG-Fusion)
md: Multi-query fusion has costs. In the Infineon study RAG-Fusion averaged 34.62 s versus 19.52 s for plain RAG (1.77 times slower in that deployment), mostly from the larger answer call, and some answers strayed off topic when the generated queries were not relevant enough. If the rewrites are near-duplicates, fusion just re-counts the same list.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
md: Two ways to use an object you did not allocate: hold an `ARef<T>` when you need it to stay alive *across time* (stored in a struct, sent to another thread), or borrow it under an `rcu::Guard` when you only need it *briefly* and the data is RCU-protected. The first costs a refcount increment; the second costs almost nothing but forbids sleeping until the guard is dropped.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: Inserting a task into a local DSQ is a commitment. Once there, it waits for that CPU even if another CPU goes idle a microsecond later. Schedulers that want work sharing keep tasks in a shared custom DSQ and move them to a local DSQ only when a CPU asks via `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
md: Misconception: if no idle CPU was found, a busy CPU will pick the task up soon. Only CPUs that run their dispatch path do, and idle tracking races with CPUs going idle. Inserting into a queue no CPU will look at, with no kick, is how schedulers stall while CPUs idle.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Hard-coded credentials (CWE-798) and why deleting them fails
md: Environment variables are a stepping stone, not the goal. OWASP's Secrets Management Cheat Sheet warns that environment variables "are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps". Prefer files or APIs that the platform injects at runtime, readable only by the one process that needs them.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
md: A misconception: "the tests pass, so it is safe". Tests show the code does what was intended for the inputs someone thought of. A security review asks about inputs nobody thought of. Every bug in this course passed its author's tests.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
md: Patterns written to *detect* attacks are code too. Cloudflare's outage came from a security rule, deployed globally within seconds because security rules must ship fast. Review regexes in WAF rules, input validators and log parsers with the same care as application code, and test them against long near-miss strings, not only against strings that match.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe
md: Review unsafe Rust as C, with one question: can any input from safe code make this block break its preconditions? Require a SAFETY comment that names the check, keep the block tiny, think about panics in the middle, and run the tests under Miri.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IKEv2: four messages to build the keys and the first tunnel
md: IKE_SA_INIT agrees on keys but proves nothing about who is on the other end; a man-in-the-middle could complete it. Authentication happens only in IKE_AUTH, where AUTH binds each peer's credential to the earlier messages. If AUTH is weak (a guessable pre-shared key), the whole tunnel is weak, however strong the Diffie-Hellman group.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
md: Architecture is placement. For each trust boundary, name the enforcement point, check that nothing can go around it, and list what it depends on. Those dependencies are your trusted computing base, and they deserve the most scrutiny.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: NIST SP 800-207: the logical architecture of zero trust
md: Zero trust concentrates trust in the policy engine, the administrator, the identity provider and the device inventory. Protect them as the most critical systems you run, and treat a change to access policy as a security event.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Queues: acknowledge fast, process later, expect duplicates
md: A longer visibility timeout reduces duplicates from slow workers. It never removes duplicates from storage redundancy or redelivery. The handler must be safe to run twice, whatever the queue settings.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: AI for finding bugs, reviewing code and writing detections
md: A rule that never fires looks exactly like a quiet network. Every detection, human or AI written, ships with samples it must match and samples it must not.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
md: "Zero-day" describes the defenders' situation (no fix existed), not how clever the attack is. Most real breaches use **known** vulnerabilities with patches available for weeks or years. Equifax (lesson 8) is the textbook example.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Defence in depth: layers, and why they must be independent
md: Defence in depth means several *different* layers across Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, so that one failure does not mean total failure. The math only works when layers fail independently: hunt down shared passwords, shared admin accounts and silent monitoring first.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Maturity models: measuring where you are with C2M2 levels
md: A maturity score measures capability, not outcomes. A domain at MIL3 can still miss an intrusion, and self-evaluations drift upward when the people scoring are the people judged. Ask for evidence for each "Fully Implemented", and pair the maturity view with outcome metrics (lesson 8).

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Designing the team: functions, coverage and where people sit
md: Single points of failure apply to people. If one engineer is the only person who understands the detection pipeline or the privileged access management (PAM) vault that holds admin passwords, the programme fails when they go on leave or resign. Recall from the appsec course how Equifax's patch alert went to a mailing list for roles that had no named owner. Pair people, document runbooks, rotate duties.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing is a security control: Equifax's patch email
md: A security message is a control with a single point of failure: the reader. Write it to one accountable person, say what to do and by when, and say what happens if they do not answer.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Writing for disclosure: vendor reports, advisories and Project Zero
md: Disclosure writing is for action: give the vendor everything needed to reproduce and fix, give the public what they need to know if they are affected and what to do, and state your timeline at the start.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
md: SPIN's fixed point is the human data distribution. It can extract more from an SFT dataset than plain SFT does, but it cannot surpass that data: once the model's responses are indistinguishable from the human ones, the loss gives no signal.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
md: They stack. Check the semantic cache first; on a miss, send a request whose stable content comes first so the provider's prefix cache can reuse it. Prompt caching is safe to turn on everywhere; a semantic cache needs the threshold and scoping work from the previous lessons.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
md: Turning off DTDs (DOCTYPE declarations) removes the whole feature: no DTD, no entity declarations, so no external entity fetch and no billion laughs. OWASP's first rule is to disable DTDs whenever possible, and to keep XInclude off too, since it loads documents without any DTD. If a format truly needs DTDs, disable external entities and external DTD loading explicitly, and keep the parser library up to date.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: HiCache: a radix tree that spans GPU, host memory and storage
md: HiCache turns GPU eviction into demotion. The radix tree, match rules and leaves-first eviction stay the same; each node simply remembers which tiers hold its KV, and a hit in host memory costs a copy instead of a prefill.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance
md: Common misconception: Dijkstra "heads toward" the target. It does not look at the target at all until it pops it. It settles every node closer than t, in all directions, which on a road map is a disc around s whose radius is the trip length.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
md: Zero-padding does not improve resolution. Smith: padding a 256-point signal to 2048 points gives 1025 spectrum samples, but "the added zeros don't change the shape of the spectrum, they only provide more samples in the frequency domain." To separate two close frequencies you need a longer *recording*.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
md: Lanes cannot branch, so SIMD code computes both sides, builds a per-lane mask with a compare, and selects. AVX2 keeps masks in vector registers and uses blendv and movemask; AVX-512 has mask registers k0 to k7 with merge or zero masking, which also handles loop tails.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
md: Slab = one cache per object size or type, slabs of whole pages cut into equal objects, a refcount per slab for trivial reclaim, and objects kept constructed between uses. It removes most of both internal and external fragmentation for small, frequent objects.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
md: A resumed partial sample can contain tokens generated by several weight versions. `--mask-offpolicy-in-partial-rollout` removes the old prefix tokens from the loss, but the docs note this does not remove the prefix-distribution mismatch: the newer tokens that are trained were still generated after a prefix the current policy might not have written.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery
md: Judge a run in order: responses, reward and log probs, mismatch, staleness, with a held-out eval from the start. Save on an interval you can afford to lose, keep straw or rollout dumps for the batches in between, and resubmit failed training to the same Ray cluster instead of tearing it down.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Reentrancy: The DAO and checks-effects-interactions
md: `transfer()` and `send()` forward only a 2,300 gas stipend, which once blocked most re-entry. Do not treat that as the fix: the Solidity docs say the stipend "might change with future hard forks", and recipients that need more gas then break. Use CEI, a guard, or both.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The four triage questions, and the decision flow they make
md: "Expected" needs evidence: a ticket, a calendar entry, a confirmation through a channel the attacker does not control. "The user is an admin, admins do this" is a guess. Attackers who steal admin accounts do exactly what admins do.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
md: Do not "watch it to learn more" once you see encryption or recovery tampering. Every minute of observation costs files. Escalate immediately with what you know, isolate if your playbook allows it, and let incident response decide about wider containment.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
md: Do not ask people to detect lies in real time. Give them a rule that does not depend on the caller being honest, and make following the rule faster than arguing.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
md: The people layer is defended by design (processes that do not depend on spotting lies), by technology that makes mistakes harmless, and by a culture where reporting is fast, safe and thanked. Blame breaks all three.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
md: A latent's name comes from what it reads (activating examples across the whole activation range, plus its density) and what it writes (its logit effect). Automated pipelines write names with one LLM and score them with another by simulation, detection or fuzzing; all of these are correlational, so finish with a causal check.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Interpolation is not the same as smoothing. Most of these methods are *exact*: the surface passes through every reading. That is right for precise instruments and wrong for noisy cheap sensors, where you want a method that can treat part of each reading as measurement error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Choose interpolators by held-out error, not by reputation. Leave-one-out RMSE (or blocked cross-validation, which holds out whole regions so test points are not right next to training points) compares methods on your data, and the standardized errors tell you whether kriging's uncertainty can be trusted.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Self-speculation: MTP heads, layer skipping and lookahead
md: Self-speculation trades a separate draft for a cheaper pass of the target: MTP modules built into training, a subset of layers, or n-grams harvested from Jacobi iterations. Cheap drafts only help if they agree with the full model, so the methods that pay off either train for it (MTP, LayerSkip) or search for it (Draft & Verify, lookahead).

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Long-form and streaming ASR are decoding problems layered on a fixed-window model: the window moves by predicted timestamps, unstable text waits for agreement, and silence must be removed or detected before the decoder invents something to say.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
md: Fast allocators round requests to size classes, serve each class from same-size slabs or spans, and put a lock-free per-thread or per-CPU cache in front. The costs are bounded rounding waste, memory parked in caches, and spans pinned by a few live objects.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
md: Clean file pages are cheap to evict, dirty ones need write-back, and anonymous ones need swap. The kernel approximates LRU with reference bits and active/inactive lists, but once the working set exceeds RAM, even a 0.1 percent miss rate makes memory 100 times slower: thrashing.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Misconception: "out of order is rare, so I can ignore it". In the toy, 5 of 12 readings arrive after a reading with a later event time. Mobile, battery-powered and intermittently connected devices make this the normal case, not an edge case.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: The Transformer's core bet: replace the recurrent chain with attention, so every position can read every other position in one layer and the whole layer runs as parallel matrix multiplications.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
md: A Transformer layer = attention (mix across positions) + FFN (transform each position), each wrapped in a residual connection and LayerNorm, with positional information added once at the input.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: Length normalization is relative to avgdl, so only a document's length compared with the average matters. An average-length document scores the same for every b.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
md: The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: The gradient points in the direction of **steepest ascent**, and its length is that steepest rate. So $-\nabla f$ is the direction of steepest descent, the direction every gradient-based **optimizer** (the algorithm that updates the parameters during training) starts from.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
md: Gradient checks can fail for honest reasons: at a kink (a sharp corner) such as ReLU at 0 (lesson 2) or a max with ties, the function is not differentiable and the two sides disagree. Check at random points away from kinks, and in double precision.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
md: Misconception: `2>&1` *links* stderr to stdout permanently. It does not. It is a one-time copy of fd 1 as it is at that moment. Any later change to fd 1 leaves fd 2 where it was.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Job control and signals: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, background jobs and trap
md: Ctrl-C is SIGINT, Ctrl-Z is SIGTSTP, `kill` is SIGTERM, `kill -9` is SIGKILL, and a closed terminal is SIGHUP. In a script, route every way out, signals included, through one `trap ... EXIT` cleanup.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Evaluating and visualizing an embedding space
md: A t-SNE plot shows neighbourhoods, not geometry. Do not conclude that one cluster is more varied than another, or that two clusters are closer than a third, from the picture. Check such claims with distances computed in the original space.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights: quantizing stores each weight in fewer bits, so 8-bit weights halve the bytes; the next lesson) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, lesson 6).

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: When one GPU is not enough: tensor parallelism and the decode floor
md: Tensor parallelism divides each token's weight bytes across T GPUs, so the decode floor falls about as 1/T, but every layer adds two all-reduces whose latency does not shrink. MoE models read only the active experts at batch 1, yet must hold all of them.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Simplified: real CPUs pipeline and overlap many instructions, and even execute them out of order (lesson 7). But they are built so that the visible result is exactly as if each instruction ran one at a time in program order, which is why this model is the right one to reason with.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
md: Misconception: "fewer instructions always means faster code." The two versions of the threshold loop do about the same work per element, yet one ran several times slower on random data. Predictability of branches, like the memory access pattern in lesson 6, can matter more than the instruction count.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT = pretraining loss + chat template + loss only on response tokens (including the end-of-turn token) + a small, high-quality dataset.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index alone does not rank anything. Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set: a document either matches or it does not. Ranking needs term weights, which lessons 6 and 7 add on top of the same postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: tf rewards a term repeated inside the document; idf rewards a term that is rare across the collection. TF-IDF multiplies them, so a match counts most when the term is frequent here and rare elsewhere.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
md: C is small: a handful of types, operators that work on bits and integers as directly as the CPU does, and `if`, `for`, `while`, `switch` and functions. What makes it hard is not syntax but the rules for memory, which the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
md: `void *` carries an address without a type; the code that receives it must convert it back to the right type. A function pointer carries code. Together they let one function such as qsort work on any data, with the caller supplying the type-specific part.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership answers C's question *who frees this, and when?* statically: the single owner frees it, at the end of the owner's scope. No `free` calls, no collector.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
md: Lifetime annotations do not change how long anything lives. They describe relationships between references so the borrow checker can verify each call site. The function body is checked against the signature, and callers are checked against the signature alone.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
md: $\det A$ is the factor by which $A$ scales areas (negative if it flips orientation). $\det A = 0$ means a direction is squashed flat: no inverse. Otherwise $A^{-1}A = I$ and $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, but in code you call `solve`, and you watch the condition number, not the determinant.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: A loss turns "fit the data" into one number that depends on the parameters. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood for class probabilities. Training means minimizing it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Watch the **gap** between training and test (or validation: a held-out split used for tuning, see lesson 8) error. A small gap with high error means underfitting; a low training error with a large gap means overfitting. Training loss alone cannot tell you which you have.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Suspiciously good validation results are a bug report until proven otherwise. Check that every preprocessing step was fit on training rows only, that no group or time period straddles the split, and that no feature is recorded after the outcome it predicts.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
md: Backprop = for each node in reverse order: upstream gradient times local gradient, summed over every path that leaves the node. One backward sweep yields the gradient for every input at once.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: Locks are for mutual exclusion; condition variables are for waiting until shared state changes. With a CV, always hold the lock, keep the condition in a state variable, and wait in a while loop. A semaphore can play either role, depending on its initial value.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
md: Data journaling writes every data block twice, which halves sequential write bandwidth. That is why metadata (ordered) journaling is the more common choice; OSTEP notes that Windows NTFS and SGI's XFS use forms of it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. The **covariance** $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]$, the mean product of the two deviations from their means, is positive when the two rise together and negative when one is high as the other is low. Lesson 8 develops it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: With little data the prior drives the answer, so state it. A prior that puts zero probability on some value can never recover it: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, and anything times 0 stays 0.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Comparing systems honestly: judgment holes, variance, significance
md: A test collection is a measuring instrument with known biases. Report the metric, cutoff and gain you used, look at per-query results, test significance with paired tests, and be suspicious when a genuinely new kind of system loses on an old pool.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: Contrastive training with in-batch negatives is what turns a language model into an embedding model: pull each true pair together, push everything else in the batch apart, with a scale (temperature) that controls how sharply.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
md: Tokenization fixes what the model can see. Vocabulary size trades sequence length against parameters; the regex and digit rules shape arithmetic; the training data mix decides which languages are cheap; and rare tokens can be under-trained.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Accumulation is exactly equivalent only for layers that treat examples independently. **BatchNorm** computes statistics per micro-batch: with examples (1, 2, 3, 4) in one batch it normalizes the value 2 to -0.45, but in the micro-batch (1, 2) it becomes +1.00. The playbook also notes that accumulation gives no throughput benefit, since it runs the same small batches; it only changes the effective batch size.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
md: Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; the last lesson shows how libraries and disk-based systems handle them.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
md: A lockfile only protects installs that use it. A Dockerfile that copies only package.json, `npx some-tool`, a global install, or a developer running `npm update` all resolve ranges fresh. The axios post-mortem told users who were "pinned to a clean version" and ran no fresh install in the window that they were fine.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
md: The xz attack was a trust attack, not a technical exploit of git, signing or builds. Every step was done by a legitimate maintainer with legitimate rights. Defences are partly social: fund and share maintenance of critical projects, add second reviewers for releases, and treat sudden pressure to hand over control or upgrade fast as a warning sign.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
md: Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Every `read` and `write` may block, move fewer bytes than asked, or fail with `EINTR` or `EAGAIN`. Loop until all bytes are moved, retry on `EINTR`, and treat `EAGAIN` as "wait until the descriptor is ready".

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: strace shows which calls a program makes and how often; getrusage shows the page faults that strace cannot see; seccomp turns a list of needed calls into an enforced allow-list. All three work on syscall numbers and miss the vDSO.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: How a mobile network fits together: radio, core and the HLR
md: The home HLR/HSS holds each subscriber's secret key and current location, and other networks must be able to query it for roaming to work. Mobile security is largely about who is allowed to ask it what.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SIM and eSIM: the key in your pocket, and how it gets there
md: The SIM is a computer that holds the subscriber's key and runs code. Protect what can reach it (filter OTA and binary SMS) and treat every way of putting a number onto a new card or eSIM as a credential reset.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Detecting GNSS spoofing, and authenticated navigation signals
md: Spoofing is caught by inconsistency: with physics, with your own clock's history, with other receivers and other time sources. Signing the navigation data (OSNMA) raises the bar, and a backup timing source keeps you running while you investigate.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time scaling has two halves that can fail independently. **Coverage**: does any attempt contain a correct answer? **Precision**: can you pick it out? The next two lessons take them one at a time.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Tree search for reasoning: Tree of Thoughts, MCTS, inference laws
md: Tree search pays when you have a step-level evaluator you can trust (code that runs, a checked answer, a strong PRM) and when early mistakes are expensive, as in Game of 24. With a weak evaluator, more search mostly finds the evaluator's mistakes, the over-optimization seen in lesson 5. And always compare at equal compute: rollouts are not free.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
md: One step of online gradient descent (one gradient step per token, in arrival order) on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong through false sharing.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
md: LOTL hunts are baseline hunts in disguise. The tools are legitimate, so the evidence is never the tool alone: it is the tool used by an account, on a host, at a time, or in a sequence that this environment has not seen before.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
md: Do not average the two grades into one number, and do not let the letter drive the digit. "A5" (a reliable source passing on something improbable) is a perfectly valid and useful grade: it tells the reader to check before acting, whoever sent it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Writing an intelligence product people act on
md: A good intelligence product states a judgement, says how likely and how sure in standard words, shows the evidence and its grade, tells each reader what to do and by when, admits its gaps, and asks for feedback. Everything else in CTI exists to make that page right.
